88-004.r: All four on UNESCO World Heritage List → Champaner-Pavagarh Archaeological Park (Panchmahal, Gujarat), Chhatrapati Shivaji station (Mumbai), Mamallapuram, Konark Sun Temple.

88-005.r: Jaipur (capital of Rajasthan) → 'Pink City', also called 'Paris of India'.

88-006.r: Wrong pair: Jaisalmer – City of Lakes; Udaipur is the City of Lakes. Jaipur → Pink City; Ujjain → City of Mahakal; Kolkata → City of Joy.

88-007.r: Tirupati's Lord Venkateswara temple → Seshachalam range, Andhra Pradesh; not on Shevaroy, Javadhu (Tamil Nadu) or Biligiriranga (Karnataka) hills → book gives no single answer (*).

88-008.r: Lord Ranganatha (Venkatesha) temple → Biligiriranga Hills, south-eastern Karnataka; possibly the only standing form of Ranganatha.
88-008.t: Don't mix up with Tirupati's Venkateswara temple, which is in the Seshachalam range of Andhra Pradesh.

88-009.r: Ministry of Tourism → promotes India with the 'Incredible India' concept.

88-010.r: Sabarimala temple (Lord Ayyappa; most famous Sastha temple) → Kerala.

88-011.r: Ghost towns (abandoned towns) → Kuldhara, Dhanushkodi, Lakhpat; Charkhari (Mahoba, UP) is not one, it is called 'Kashmir of Bundelkhand'.

88-012.r: Only correct: Srisailam (Mallikarjuna jyotirlinga, Kurnool) → Nallamala Hills. Omkareshwar → Mandhata island in Narmada (Khandwa), not Satmala Hills; Pushkar is not on Mahadeo Hills.

88-013.r: Banni grassland → Gujarat; Bugyal grassland → Uttarakhand; Khajjiar → Himachal Pradesh; Pahalgam → Jammu & Kashmir.

89-001.r: Biogas plants → give both power and manure; biogas forms when organic matter (farm waste, manure, sewage) breaks down without oxygen.

89-002.r: Speed Post Service → started by India Post in August 1986; time-bound express delivery, charges refunded if late.

89-003.r: Wrong: India 'second' in nitrogenous fertilizers; it was third then (and ninth in steel). Now India is second in crude steel and in coal after China (2022).

89-006.r: Wrong pair: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre is in Maharashtra, not Karnataka. Sriharikota → Andhra Pradesh; Thumba → Kerala; Pokhran → Rajasthan.

89-007.r: Towns near Mumbai: Alibag → holiday resort; Balapur → petro-chemical complex; Nhava Sheva → fully mechanized port; Ratnagiri → fishing centre.

89-008.r: Chandipur (Odisha) → sea recedes a few km from the shore twice a day at ebb tide, so one can walk on the sea floor.

89-009.r: Thumba (Thiruvananthapuram) → chosen for TERLS rocket station (1963, Vikram Sarabhai, INCOSPAR) because it lies close to the geomagnetic equator.

89-011.r: Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya → Raipur, Chhattisgarh (not Rajasthan); Acharya NG Ranga Agriculture University → Andhra Pradesh (not Telangana); two wrong pairs → book gives no single answer (*).

89-012.r: Cairn Energy (now Capricorn Energy), oil and gas explorer → headquarters in Edinburgh, Scotland.

89-013.r: Rameshwaram → Tamil Nadu; Dwarka → Gujarat; Sarnath (Varanasi) → Uttar Pradesh; Mahakal Temple (Ujjain) → Madhya Pradesh.

89-014.r: Stadiums: Aish Bagh → Bhopal; Brabourne → Mumbai; Green Park → Kanpur; Eden Gardens → Kolkata.

89-015.r: Underground railway → Calcutta (India's first metro); mangoes → Ratnagiri; locks → Aligarh; rice → Dehradun.

89-016.r: Diamond Harbour and Salt Lake City → Kolkata (West Bengal).

89-017.r: Dindigul → city (district) in Tamil Nadu; Haider Ali set up a modern arsenal there with French help.

89-018.r: Green Highway (Plantation, Transplantation, Beautification and Maintenance) Policy 2015 → planting trees along all highways; helps environment, local people, jobs.

89-019.r: Wrong pair: Kutch – forest resources (Kutch has no forest resources). Kolhan → mineral; Malabar Coast → water; Middle Ganga Plain → soil resources.

89-020.r: Moradabad ('Peetal Nagri') → brassware and glassware, not sarees; Chanderi, Banarasi, Kanjivaram → sarees.

89-021.r: Wrong pair: Dr. M.S. Swaminathan ('Father of the Green Revolution') → agriculture, not geology. Manmohan Singh → economics; A.P.J. Abdul Kalam → aeronautics; D.S. Kothari → physics.

89-022.r: Jangal Mahal → West Bengal; in the news for Naxalite activities.

89-023.r: Apsara → India's first nuclear reactor, working from August 1956 at BARC, Trombay (Mumbai).
89-023.h: Apsara begins with 'A', the first letter — India's first reactor.

89-024.r: Telegraph 1850 (Calcutta–Diamond Harbour); telephone exchanges 1881; first formal telephone service 28 January 1882 → no option fits, so the book gives no single answer (*).

89-025.r: Wrong pair: Lasundra hot spring is in Gujarat, not Rajasthan. Avloli → Maharashtra; Manikaran → Himachal Pradesh; Sohna → Haryana.

89-026.r: Chapchar Kut festival (March, after jhoom forest clearing) → Mizoram; Khongjom Parba ballad and Thang-Ta martial dance → Manipur, not Sikkim.

89-027.r: Puthukkuli shawls (Todas, Nilgiris) → Tamil Nadu; Sujni embroidery → Bihar (not Maharashtra); Uppada Jamdani saris → Andhra Pradesh (not Karnataka).

89-028.r: Himalayan nettle (Girardinia diversifolia) → sustainable source of textile fibre; grows in the Himalayas and Hindukush.

89-029.r: May–June dust storms in Rajasthan → caused by convection currents at some places only; not Aravalli alignment or fast easterly winds.

90-001.r: Big Bang Theory → origin of the Universe; given by Georges Lemaitre; universe began as a hot, dense point about 13.7–13.8 billion years ago.

90-002.r: Big Bang Theory → explains the origin of the universe; age of universe about 13.7–13.8 billion years.

90-003.r: Continental drift theory → Alfred Wegener, German geophysicist.

90-004.r: Milky Way → a spiral galaxy; each galaxy holds about 100 billion stars; our solar system lies in the Milky Way.

90-005.r: Sun takes about 25 crore years to revolve once around the centre of the Milky Way; it lies about 7.94 kpc from the galactic centre.

90-006.r: Star colour → shows its temperature: blue hottest (50,000–28,000 K), then blue-white, white, yellow (6000–4900 K), orange, red coolest (3500–2000 K).

90-007.r: Chandrasekhar limit → maximum mass of a white dwarf, about 1.44 solar masses; above it a star collapses into a neutron star or black hole; Nobel Prize 1983.

90-008.r: Black hole → a collapsed star; most form from remains of a large star dying in a supernova (NASA); black hole theory → S. Chandrasekhar.

90-011.r: Black hole first explained by S. Chandrasekhar (Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 solar masses); Nobel Prize in Physics.

90-012.r: S. Chandrashekhar → presented the idea of a white dwarf turning into a black hole on 11 January 1935 (Royal Astronomical Society, London); Nobel Prize 1983 with W.A. Fowler.

90-013.r: Black hole cannot be seen by telescope → its intense gravity (high density) lets no radiation, not even light, escape; A and R true, R explains A.

90-015.r: Supernova → huge explosion at the end of a star's life (a dying star); happens in binary star systems or at the end of a single star's life.

90-016.r: There are 88 constellations in the sky (International Astronomical Union); most are seen from the southern hemisphere.

90-017.r: Brittle star → sea animal (echinoderm, class Ophiuroidea, related to starfish), not astronomical; pulsar, quasar and black hole are astronomical objects.

90-018.r: Pulsar, black hole, quasar → found in space; Brittle Star → a sea echinoderm related to starfish.
90-018.t: Don't be fooled by 'star' in Brittle Star; it is a sea creature.

90-019.r: Constellation → group of stars forming a recognizable pattern, named after its shape or a mythological figure.

90-020.r: Betelgeuse (second-brightest star of Orion, about 700 light years away) → first star other than the Sun directly imaged by Hubble.

90-021.r: In space between Earth and Sun: sky looks black and stars don't twinkle (no atmosphere); outside temperature (about 2.7 K) is far below Earth's.

90-022.r: Light year → unit of distance: the distance light travels in vacuum in one year, about 9.461 trillion km.

90-023.r: Light year → unit for distances between stars; distance light covers in one year in vacuum at about 3 lakh km per second.

90-024.r: Stars rise perpendicular to the horizon for an observer at the Equator, where the celestial equator is nearly overhead.

90-025.r: Pole star shines in the north; to walk east, keep the pole star on your left.
90-025.h: Face east and north is always on your left hand.

90-026.r: Saptarishi → group of stars that shows the direction of the pole (pole star).

90-027.r: Byte (group of eight bits) → computer term; telemetering, weightlessness and cislunar → space terms.

90-028.r: Event Horizon (boundary around a black hole), Singularity, String Theory, Standard Model → terms about observing and understanding the Universe.

90-029.r: Standard time → official time of a region or country, not a natural unit; day, lunar month, tropical year are natural units.

91-001.r: Nebula → not part of the solar system; solar system (formed about 4.6 billion years ago) has the Sun, planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, meteoroids.

91-002.r: Copernicus (Poland) → first gave the Heliocentric Theory (Sun at centre, Earth revolves) in 'Commentariolus'; book notes Varahamihira gave the idea in the sixth century.

91-005.r: Nicholas Copernicus → first established that all planets, including Earth, revolve around the Sun.

91-006.r: Earth → densest planet (5.5 g/cm³; Mercury 5.4, Venus 5.2); Earth's main element is iron (32.07%), then oxygen (30.12%), silicon (15.12%).

91-007.r: Old count 9 planets; order from Sun → Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (then Pluto); Earth 149.6 million km from Sun.
91-007.h: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles' = Mercury to Neptune in order.

91-012.r: Planets → non-luminous bodies that shine by reflecting the Sun's light.

91-013.r: Smallest planet → Pluto (old list; now Mercury); largest → Jupiter; second from Sun → Venus; nearest to Sun → Mercury.

91-015.r: Wrong pair: slowest planet is Neptune, not Mars (one revolution in 60190 Earth days, about 165 years). Largest → Jupiter; smallest → Mercury; brightest → Venus.

91-016.r: Planet size, decreasing: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury.
91-016.h: Giants first J-S-U-N ('JSUN'), then Earth, Venus, Mars, Mercury.

91-017.r: Hydrogen, helium, methane → main gases of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune; no option lists exactly these → book gives no single answer (*).

91-018.r: Florida → a state of the USA, not a planet; Mercury, Venus, Saturn are planets.

91-019.r: Goldilocks Zone → habitable zone around a star, not too hot or cold, where liquid water can exist; used in search for Earth-like planets.

91-020.r: Uranus → planet; Moon → natural satellite; Halley → comet; Mariner → artificial satellite.

91-021.r: True: Neptune has sub-zero methane gas rings; Mars's moons are Phobos and Deimos. False: hottest planet is Venus (about 464 °C); Ganymede belongs to Jupiter.

91-022.r: Sun → chief heavenly body, at the centre of the solar system.

92-001.r: Sun's centre (about 15,000,000 °C) → matter only as gas and plasma (fourth state of matter); no option fits → book gives no single answer (*).

92-002.r: Solar energy → nuclear fusion: small nuclei (hydrogen) combine into heavier helium, releasing energy; fission splits a heavy nucleus.

92-003.r: Diamond ring effect → at the start and end of totality in a total solar eclipse, as last sunlight passes lunar valleys; book's answer: peripheral regions of totality trail.
92-003.c: The book prints (c), but its own explanation says the diamond ring appears at the beginning and end of totality, which matches options (a) and (b).

92-004.r: Solar eclipse → only on New Moon day (Amavasya), when the Moon comes between Earth and Sun and its shadow falls on Earth.
92-004.t: Full Moon (Poornima) is the trap option; a solar eclipse needs a New Moon.

92-007.r: Total solar eclipse seen only in limited regions → the Moon's shadow on Earth is small compared to Earth's cross-section.

92-008.r: Sun's halo → refraction of sunlight by ice crystals in high cirrus clouds.

92-009.r: 1 Astronomical Unit (AU) → mean Earth–Sun distance, 149.6 million km (about 150 million km).

92-012.r: Perihelion (Earth nearest the Sun) → first week of January (about 3rd–4th January); Aphelion (farthest) → 4th July.

92-013.r: Sun's diameter → about 109 times Earth's (109.2, NASA); mean radius: Sun 695700 km, Earth 6371 km.

92-014.r: Both false: Earth's rotation (west to east) → day and night; revolution around the Sun → seasons.
92-014.h: Rotation = daily Routine (day-night); Revolution = yearly Round (seasons).

92-015.r: Photosphere → bright visible layer of the Sun above the convection zone; innermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere; temperature around 5500 °C.

93-001.r: Mercury's kinetic energy is greatest at the orbit point nearest the Sun (A): stronger solar pull makes it move fastest there.

93-002.r: Mercury → shortest orbit, 88 days; Venus 224.7 days; Earth 365.2; Mars 687; Jupiter 11.86 years; Saturn 29.4; Uranus 84.07; Neptune 164.9 years.

93-003.r: Mercury and Venus → no moons; Earth 1, Mars 2, Jupiter 95, Saturn 146, Uranus 27, Neptune 14 moons.

93-004.r: Albedo → reflectivity that sets an object's brightness in reflected light; Mercury's albedo (about 0.1) is lower than Earth's (about 0.3).

94-001.r: Average temperatures: Venus 464 °C (hottest), Mercury 167 °C, Earth 15 °C, Mars −65 °C; Neptune −200 °C (coldest).
94-001.t: Don't pick Mercury just because it is nearest the Sun; Venus is the hottest planet.

94-002.r: Venus → 'Evening Star' and 'Morning Star'; Mars → Red Planet; Saturn → lowest density, lighter than water.

94-003.r: Venus → 'Morning Star' and 'Evening Star' (brightest planet); also Earth's 'twin sister' (similar size, mass, composition).

94-004.r: Human life on Venus unlikely → atmosphere about 96.5% carbon dioxide and surface above 400 °C; A and R true, R explains A.

94-005.r: Venus → Earth's twin sister (sister planet); also the brightest planet, Morning Star and Evening Star.

94-006.r: Magellan spacecraft → Venus surface-mapping mission; launched 04 May 1989, reached Venus orbit 10 August 1990; named after explorer Ferdinand Magellan.

95-001.r: Aristotle (384-322 BC) → first to describe Earth as spherical, in 'On the Heavens'; Ptolemy, Strabo and Copernicus came later.

95-002.r: Earth → called the 'Green Planet' because of the life and ecology on it.

95-003.r: Earth's equatorial diameter → 12,756 km (about 12,800 km); polar diameter → 12,714 km.

95-004.r: Weight is least at the Equator (strongest centrifugal force) and most at the Poles → A false; Earth is an oblate spheroid, not a perfect sphere → R true.

95-005.r: Moon's core → solid, unlike Earth's fluid core.

95-006.r: Earth's crust by weight: oxygen 46.60% (most), silicon 27.72%, aluminium 8.13%, iron 5.00%, calcium 3.63%.

95-007.r: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth; nearest option: 8 minutes.

95-008.r: Sunlight reaches Earth in about 8 minutes 19 seconds (499.0 seconds).

95-009.r: Sun → nearest star to Earth (149.6 million km); next Alpha Centauri (4.35 light years); Sirius A 8.6 ly; Polaris 434 ly (new estimate 323).

95-010.r: Nearest planet to Earth: Venus (41.4 million km), then Mars (78.4 million km); when Venus is not an option, answer Mars.

95-012.r: Earth's revolution → about 365.25 days (365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes); tropical (solar) year = 365.24 days.

95-013.r: Earth's average orbital speed → 29.8 km/s (about 30 km/s); Mercury 47.4, Venus 35, Mars 24.1, Jupiter 13.1 km/s.

95-014.r: Earth's equatorial circumference about 40,000 km (40,090.28 km); rotation speed about 1670 km/h = 27.8 km/min → no option fits, book gives no single answer (*).

95-016.r: Earth's axis of rotation (through North and South Poles) → always inclined at 23.5° (option d).

95-017.r: Only true: Earth's magnetic equator passes through Thumba. Magnetic axis is not uniformly at 23½°; north magnetic pole was on Queen Elizabeth Island (Canada), not a peninsula.

95-018.r: True: northern end of Earth's axis → North Pole; Earth's axis stays parallel. False: 45° parallel (28343.892 km) is not half the equator (40090.28 km); not faster at aphelion.

95-019.r: Day and night → caused by Earth's rotation on its axis (about 24 hours per rotation).

95-020.r: Sun's rays fall vertically on the Equator on 21 March and 23 September → day and night equal (12 hours each) in both hemispheres.

95-021.r: Seasons → Earth's revolution around the Sun plus axial tilt of 23½°; changing Earth–Sun distance matters only slightly.

95-023.r: Noon is hotter in summer → in winter the Sun's rays fall more slanting on the surface; not because Earth is closer to the Sun.

95-024.r: If Sun–Earth distance shrank by a quarter → smaller orbit and faster revolution → year shorter than 365.25 days.

95-025.r: A false: not every satellite goes east (polar-orbit satellites launch north or south). R true: Earth rotates west to east, giving eastward launches extra momentum.

95-026.r: A ball thrown out of an orbiting satellite → keeps revolving around Earth in the same orbit and period as the satellite.

95-027.r: Earth's inner layer NIFE → mainly nickel and ferrum (iron).

95-028.r: Earth's core → mainly iron: outer core about 2260 km thick (liquid iron and nickel); inner core a hot dense iron ball, radius about 1220 km.

95-029.r: Earth Day → 22 April every year; first celebrated in 1970, birth of the modern environmental movement.

95-031.r: Earth's axis → tilted about 23½°; Earth rotates at about 1037 miles per hour, one rotation in about 24 hours.

95-032.r: True: Earth's magnetic field reverses every few hundred thousand years; early life modified the early atmosphere. False: early Earth had no free oxygen, not 54%.

95-033.r: Aryabhatta → first to explain that Earth's rotation on its axis causes daily sunrise and sunset; works compiled in Aryasiddhanta.

95-034.r: Deserts most likely near 23° latitude → tropical arid belt mostly 15–30°; high pressure near 30° latitude (Sahara, Australian deserts).

96-001.r: Mars → day 24 h 37 min and axial tilt 25°12′, almost the same as Earth's (23 h 56 min; 23°30′).

96-002.r: Mars takes longer than Earth to orbit (687.0 vs 365.256 days), being farther (228 vs 149.6 million km) → A false; Mars is smaller (6792 km) → R true.

96-003.r: Ice caps and frozen water → most relevant for life on Mars; Mars air: 95.1% carbon dioxide, 2.59% nitrogen, 1.94% argon, 0.16% oxygen.

96-004.r: Book gives two answers: Mars and Europa (Jupiter's ice-covered moon with a possible frozen ocean 60-150 km deep) may support alien life.

96-005.r: Phoenix Mars Lander → launched 4 August 2007, landed 25 May 2008 near Mars's North Pole, found ice; book's answer 26 May 2008 (nearest option).

97-001.r: Jupiter's four largest moons (Io, Europa, Callisto, Ganymede) → 'Galilean moons', discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610.

97-002.r: Largest planet → Jupiter (diameter 142 984 km), then Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Earth, Venus, Mars; Mercury smallest (4 879 km).

97-003.r: Jupiter → heaviest planet; diameter 142984 km, average density 1326 kg/m³; spins fastest on its axis.
